claims.text: Increasing local lattice distortion from compositional disorder enhances electron–phonon coupling in high-entropy superconducting alloys.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling raises the superconducting transition temperature.
The proposed starting material is a disordered, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
Reported Nb–Ta or titanium-rich alloys provide material systems similar to the proposed starting material.
Substitution with elements having substantially different atomic radii will increase local lattice distortion.
The radius-changing substitutions can be made while retaining a single-phase solid solution.
Comparable arc-melting and homogenization processing will ensure uniform solid-state mixing across samples.
Local lattice distortion or strain can be quantified from diffraction-derived lattice deviations or strain fields.
Compositional fluctuations create local strain fields.
Local strain fields broaden and soften the phonon spectrum.
Phonon broadening and softening increase the electron–phonon coupling constant.
Excessive disorder may impair electron mobility and become detrimental to superconductivity.
Samples with greater measured lattice distortion will have higher superconducting transition temperatures than a low-mismatch baseline alloy.
The expected increase in transition temperature is on the order of a few kelvin.
A conventional Nb–Ta-based single-phase alloy has relatively low atomic-size mismatch and an established superconducting transition temperature.
The proposed distortion–superconductivity relationship applies only while the alloy remains a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Phase separation or clustering may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
A lack of correlation between distortion, electron–phonon coupling, and transition temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention changes elemental identities through substitution, whereas the experiment calls for samples with identical overall elemental percentages but different average atomic-size mismatch. If both elemental identities and percentages are identical, average size mismatch cannot ordinarily be varied by the stated compositional route.
